slides.title: Network security
slides.say: Welcome to domain four of the Network Plus N10-009 exam: network security. It is worth fourteen percent of the exam. We will cover basic security concepts, the attacks you must recognize, and the defenses that stop them.

slides.title: 4.1 Core security concepts
items: CIA triad: confidentiality, integrity, availability
Least privilege: give only the access needed
Defense in depth: layered controls
Zero trust: verify every request
Segmentation and a screened subnet (DMZ) for public servers
Threat, vulnerability, exploit, and risk
slides.say: Start with the C I A triad: confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Least privilege means giving only the access that is needed. Defense in depth means layering controls so one failure does not expose everything. Zero trust means verifying every request. Segmentation, including a screened subnet, also called a D M Z, keeps public servers away from the internal network. And know the terms: a threat is something that can cause harm, a vulnerability is a weakness, an exploit uses the weakness, and risk is the likelihood and impact.

slides.title: 4.1 Authentication and access
head: Term
Meaning
rows: Two or more factors: know, have, are
Central AAA for network devices and users
Authenticate before a port or wireless link is usable
slides.say: For authentication, triple A means authentication, authorization, and accounting. M F A uses two or more factors, such as something you know, something you have, and something you are. S S O lets one login cover many services, and sam el is a common standard for it. Radius and tack axe plus provide central triple A for devices and users. Kerberos uses tickets, and L D A P looks up a directory. Eight oh two dot one X and N A C make a device authenticate before its port or wireless link becomes usable. And P K I provides certificates and trusted authorities.

slides.title: 4.1 Special environments
items: Geofencing: allow or block by physical location
SCADA, ICS, and OT: control industrial equipment
Keep OT and IoT on isolated segments
Legacy devices may be unpatchable, so isolate them
Time-based authentication limits when access is valid
slides.say: Some environments need special care. Geofencing allows or blocks access based on physical location. S C A D A, I C S, and O T systems control industrial equipment, and they should be on isolated segments. The same goes for I o T and legacy devices that cannot be patched. And time-based authentication limits when access is valid.

slides.title: 4.2 Denial of service and spoofing
head: Attack
How it works
rows: Flood a target until it cannot serve users
Bad DNS data sends users to the wrong site
Fill the switch table so it floods frames
Forged frames kick wireless clients off
slides.say: Now attacks. A denial of service attack floods a target until it cannot serve users, and a distributed one uses many sources. A R P poisoning sends fake A R P replies to redirect traffic. D N S poisoning plants bad D N S data so users reach the wrong site. M A C flooding fills the switch table so the switch floods frames to every port. An on-path attack, also called man in the middle, puts the attacker between two parties. And deauthentication attacks use forged frames to kick wireless clients off.

slides.title: 4.2 Rogue devices and VLAN attacks
head: Attack
How it works
rows: Hands out bad gateway and DNS settings
Unauthorized AP plugged into the network
Fake AP copying a real SSID
Double tagging or switch spoofing reach other VLANs
Tricks a person into revealing credentials
slides.say: More attacks. A rogue D H C P server hands out bad gateway and D N S settings. A rogue access point is an unauthorized access point plugged into your network. An evil twin is a fake access point that copies a real S S I D. V LAN hopping uses double tagging or switch spoofing to reach other V LANs. Phishing tricks a person into revealing credentials, and ransomware encrypts data and demands payment.

slides.title: 4.3 Defenses against switch attacks
head: Attack
Defense
rows: Disable trunking on access ports; change native VLAN
slides.say: Objective four point three is defenses. Match each attack to its defense. Port security stops M A C flooding. D H C P snooping stops rogue D H C P servers. Dynamic A R P inspection stops A R P poisoning. B P D U guard stops a rogue switch. To stop V LAN hopping, disable trunking on access ports and change the native V LAN. And shut down unused ports.

slides.title: 4.3 Network defenses
head: Control
Purpose
rows: Permit or deny; ends with an implicit deny
Decoy that attracts and studies attackers
Limit how far an attack can spread
slides.say: Network defenses. Access control lists and firewall rules permit or deny traffic, and they end with an implicit deny. An I D S detects attacks, and an I P S also blocks them. U R L and content filtering blocks categories of websites. A honeypot is a decoy that attracts and studies attackers. Segmentation limits how far an attack can spread. Change default passwords on every device, and patch to close known vulnerabilities.

slides.title: 4.3 Wireless and remote defenses
items: Use WPA3, or WPA2 with AES; avoid WEP and open networks
Use 802.1X with RADIUS for enterprise Wi-Fi
Disable unused services and ports
Encrypt remote access: SSH, VPN, TLS
Log and monitor, and review the logs
Hardening: apply a secure baseline to every device
slides.say: For wireless and remote access, use W P A three, or W P A two with A E S, and never W E P or an open network. Use eight oh two dot one X with radius for enterprise Wi-Fi. Disable unused services and ports. Encrypt remote access with S S H, a V P N, or T L S. Log and monitor, and actually review the logs. And apply a secure baseline to every device, which is called hardening.

slides.title: Domain 4 recap
items: CIA, least privilege, zero trust, AAA
Match each attack to its defense
Snooping, port security, DAI, BPDU guard
ACLs end with an implicit deny
Change defaults, patch, segment, monitor
slides.say: To recap domain four: know the C I A triad, least privilege, zero trust, and triple A. Match each attack to its defense: port security, D H C P snooping, dynamic A R P inspection, and B P D U guard. Remember that access lists end with an implicit deny. And always change defaults, patch, segment, and monitor. Good luck.
